newsitem.title: USA: FULL TEXT - HP reports Q2 results.
newsitem.headline: FULL TEXT - HP reports Q2 results.

text.p: Hewlett-Packard Co Thursday reported second quarter profits of $784 million or $0.75 cents a share. The following is a copy of the company's news release.

PALO ALTO, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--May 15, 1997--Hewlett-Packard Company (NYSE:HWP) today reported an 8 percent increase in net earnings, 5 percent growth in net revenue and a 3 percent increase in orders for the 1997 fiscal year's second quarter, which ended April 30.

Net earnings for the quarter were $784 million, or 75 cents per share, on approximately 1.05 billion shares of common stock and common-stock equivalents outstanding. This compares with earnings in the same quarter last year of $723 million, or 69 cents per share, on approximately 1.06 billion shares. (All figures for earnings per share (EPS) and number of shares and equivalents outstanding reflect the company's 2-for-1 stock split in July 1996.)

"Many aspects of our results were good, and we were able to generate good profit margins despite continued slowing in order growth," said Lewis E. Platt, HP chairman, president and chief executive officer. "Our cost-of-sales result was excellent, and we continued to make progress in managing our operating assets and in generating cash. We're disappointed, however, with order and revenue growth. A tough comparison with last year, as well as currency effects and slowing in some markets, affected our growth rates." Business Summary

Net revenue for the quarter was $10.3 billion, compared with $9.9 billion in last year's second quarter, when revenue rose 33 percent. Net revenue in the United States was $4.4 billion, an increase of 1 percent compared with the year-ago quarter, while net revenue from outside the United States rose 7 percent to $5.9 billion.

Orders for the quarter were $10.4 billion, a 3 percent increase over last year's second quarter, when orders rose 24 percent. Without the effects of currency-exchange rates, the company's order growth this quarter would have been approximately 3 percentage points higher.

In the United States, orders declined by 2 percent and were $4.6 billion, while orders from outside the United States rose 7 percent to $5.8 billion. In Europe, orders totaled $3.3 billion, down 1 percent in U.S. dollars and up 3 percent in local currency. Orders in Asia Pacific, Canada and Latin America increased 19 percent and totaled $2.5 billion. -- Computer Business

Net revenue in the computer business increased 5 percent over the same quarter last year and totaled $8.5 billion. Orders in the computer business increased 1 percent over the year-ago quarter and were $8.5 billion. The company said that its efforts to reduce PC and printer inventories in the reseller channel adversely affected this quarter's growth. -- Clients

PC workstations based on the Pentium(R) Pro microprocessor and Microsoft(R) Windows NT(R) operating system achieved a sharp order increase and modest revenue growth. Orders and revenue for UNIX(R) system workstations declined, although orders for midrange UNIX system workstations were good.

HP Vectra PCs achieved good order growth in units, but revenue was flat. Orders and revenue for the HP Pavilion home PC declined, due in large part to the fact that the year-ago quarter included major product introductions while this quarter did not. Orders and revenue for HP OmniBook notebook PCs rose very sharply, driven by recent product introductions. -- Servers
HP NetServer PCs achieved excellent order and revenue growth, with particular strength in the United States and Asia Pacific. HP NetServer LH departmental servers were especially strong.

Overall orders and revenue for UNIX system servers rose slightly. There was strength at the low end and in the midrange of the product line but weakness at the high end. Early acceptance of new technical servers from the Convex division was very good. -- Hardcopy Products

The inkjet business achieved modest order and revenue growth this quarter, due in part to slower overall growth in the worldwide inkjet market. In addition, the inkjet business faced an extremely difficult comparison with last year. However, there was strong acceptance of products in emerging inkjet categories that were introduced during the quarter, such as the HP OfficeJet Pro 1150C color all-in-one product. Inkjet supplies achieved very good growth this quarter.

Orders and revenue for HP LaserJet printers declined slightly in comparison with a very strong year-ago quarter. Demand for LaserJet personal printers was strong, and there was a modest increase in orders for LaserJet printer supplies. -- Services and Support

Order and revenue growth in the services and support business was very good in all major geographies. Demand for professional services, such as consulting and education, was excellent, and orders for software and hardware support posted moderate increases. Orders were also strong for services that help customers upgrade their desktop environments. -- Test and Measurement
Orders in the company's test-and-measurement business increased 14 percent, exceeding $1 billion for the third time in HP's history.

Order growth was broad-based across major product lines, with excellent demand for semiconductor-test equipment and instrumentation aimed at the wireless-communication industry. Additionally, fiber-optic test instruments, as well as the acceSS7 system for network monitoring, achieved healthy increases. -- Medical, Chemical Analysis and Components

Order growth for the medical-products group, at 10 percent, was consistent across product lines. The chemical-analysis business achieved a 2 percent increase, with particular strength in mass-spectrometer products. Orders in the components business grew 12 percent, driven by demand for fiber-optic, infrared and motion-control components. Costs and Expenses

Cost of goods sold this quarter was 65.2 percent of net revenue, compared with 65.8 percent in the year-ago quarter and 65.0 percent in the first quarter of fiscal 1997. "We're quite pleased with the cost-of-sales outcome," said Platt. "This is the first year-over-year decline in our cost-of-sales ratio in a very long time. There were two main drivers of this result: a shift in our revenue mix to higher-gross-margin products and continued improvements in supply-chain management."

Operating expenses rose 7 percent, compared with last year's second quarter, and were 24.1 percent of net revenue. This compares with 23.7 percent in the same quarter a year ago and 22.6 percent in the first quarter of fiscal 1997.

"While we're pleased that we reduced the rate of operating-expense growth from that of the first quarter, we didn't do quite as well as we needed to, given this quarter's slowdown in revenue growth," said Platt. "Managing operating expenses will continue to be a major focus in the months ahead." Asset Management

Return on assets for the quarter was 9.9 percent, compared with 10.3 percent in the year-ago period and 10.0 percent in the prior quarter. Inventory declined to 15.7 percent of revenue, compared with 18.7 percent in the second quarter last year and 15.8 percent in the first quarter of fiscal 1997. As a percentage of net revenue, accounts receivable also declined to 17.2 percent, compared with 19.5 percent in the same period last year and 17.4 percent in the prior quarter. Net property, plant and equipment increased to 14.6 percent of revenue, compared with 14.0 percent in the year-ago period and 14.3 percent in the prior quarter.

"We're continuing to make good progress on asset management," said Robert P. Wayman, HP executive vice president and chief financial officer. "We made strides on inventory, and our other key asset categories are at very acceptable levels. As a result, cash generation this quarter was very strong. Asset performance will remain a top priority across the company." Six-month Review

For the six months ended April 30, net earnings rose 12 percent to $1.7 billion, compared with $1.5 billion in the first half of fiscal 1996. Net earnings per share were $1.62, a 13 percent increase over the $1.44 the company earned in last year's first half. (EPS figures reflect the effect of the company's 2-for-1 stock split in July 1996.)

Net revenue increased 8 percent over the first half of last year and totaled $20.6 billion. Net revenue in the United States was $8.7 billion, an increase of 7 percent over last year's first half, while net revenue from outside the United States rose 8 percent to $11.9 billion.

Orders for the six-month period were $21.4 billion, an increase of 6 percent compared with the same period last year. U.S. orders were $8.8 billion, an increase of 2 percent, while orders from outside the United States grew 8 percent and totaled $12.6 billion. Business Outlook
"Going forward, our task is to reinvigorate growth across the company while continuing to manage costs, expenses and assets extremely well," said Platt.

"We're pursuing numerous initiatives with high growth potential. A key strategy in our computer business is to enable IT users to create what we call the extended enterprise. Customers are increasingly asking HP to help them work across physical and organizational boundaries so their employees, customers and suppliers can collaborate with unprecedented ease.

"We're working on many fronts to meet this need. We have aggressive introductions planned for UNIX system servers, hardcopy products and other businesses. We're strengthening our offerings in electronic commerce and Internet security. We're helping customers create solutions that incorporate the UNIX operating system and Microsoft Windows NT; one example is our program to integrate high-end PCs and UNIX system workstations for technical users.
"In addition, we're helping create new product categories -- such as all-in-one products and digital photography -- where our offerings have won good early acceptance.

"We also believe there is exciting growth potential in our measurement businesses," Platt continued. "For example, we're well-positioned to help healthcare providers use information technology to improve outcomes and reduce costs. Our new HP Viridia family of healthcare solutions is focused on these needs. In addition, this quarter's comeback in the semiconductor and communications industries offers significant opportunities for our test-and-measurement and components businesses.

"Although the macroeconomic environment is somewhat uncertain, and competitive conditions are intense, evolving customer needs offer many growth opportunities for HP. We believe we have the people, technologies and partnerships to turn these opportunities into growth by creating powerful solutions for customers."

Hewlett-Packard Company is a leading global provider of computing, Internet and Intranet solutions, services, communications products and measurement solutions, all of which are recognized for excellence in quality and support. It is the second-largest computer supplier in the United States, with computer-related revenue in excess of $31.4 billion in its 1996 fiscal year. HP has 114,600 employees and had revenue of $38.4 billion in its 1996 fiscal year.

This news release contains forward-looking statements, based on current expectations, that involve risks and uncertainties that could cause HP's results to differ materially. In addition to the factors discussed above, other risks include the timely development, production and acceptance of new products and services and their feature sets; the challenge of managing asset levels, including inventory; the flow of products into third-party distribution channels; and the other risks detailed from time to time in the company's Securities and Exchange Commission reports, including, but not limited to, the Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended Oct. 31, 1996, and the Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the fiscal quarter ended Jan. 31, 1997.
